toc.title: How do you keep yourself stuck?
This has nothing to do with blame
Emotions leading to behavior and cognitive adaptations

blocks.p: Wild mammals aren't traumatized, even though they live in constant life-or-death situations. They don't exist with stuck autonomic nervous systems. They can allow the natural process of self-regulation to occur, climbing to the top of their Polyvagal ladders. How is it that humans don't do the same?

Technically, we can. We still have the natural capacity to self-regulate and receive co-regulation. We seem to have lost our capacity to do so effectively day to day. It's still in us, but we've gotten really bad at it. Instead, we get stuck. A huge part of the problem is what we do to each other that keeps us stuck, like the obvious stuff: war, persecution, violence, manipulation, and on and on. (That's an enormous conversation for another time.)

There are also things we do to keep ourselves stuck. Things we do to ourselves that prevent our self-regulation. Not on purpose, of course. But still, we reinforce our stuckness. I hope you get the pieces you need to write [a new narrative](piece:build-a-new-narrative) for yourself. This can help alleviate some of the self-reinforcing stuckness.

Learning to [self-regulate](piece:regulation) is the way through. And if you can do that, you'll be much better prepared to provide co-regulation to others. If we get enough people untraumatized and co-regulating, those larger-level traumatic institutional and social things we do may lessen over time.
I'll share Bill's story and discuss some ways we keep ourselves stuck in a traumatized state. After each one, we'll identify how Bill stays stuck in trauma.

In his youth, Bill's Father, Franklin, was present physically but not emotionally. His Father did not connect with Bill; instead, Franklin focused his energy on his work. Franklin was an employee of a local business that expected him to work overtime. They made it clear he was replaceable, and they could let go of him at any time, for any reason. Bill's Mother did not have to work for income, as Bill's Father made enough for the family to get by. Franklin could not connect with Bill, overwhelmed with his focus on work. When Bill asked Franklin to color with crayons or build Lincoln Logs, he would consistently say "no" with an exasperated huff.

Bill's Father seemed to grow more distant over time. He yelled often, threw things in the house, stormed off in a huff, and isolated. He frequently asked with overwhelmed exasperation, "Can't you see I'm busy?!" and hollered about the importance of focusing on his work. "You're all depending on me; I need to focus!"

Bill got the most attention from his Father when he made a "mistake," like getting Bs at school or not using manners at the dinner table. Bill constantly felt on edge around his Father, desperately and quietly wanting to connect with him.

Now, Bill is a Father, husband, and business owner. Bill works nonstop on his business and is overwhelmed and frustrated, though it began as something he was passionate about. He initially took pride in owning his business and providing for the family; he now secretly loathes the obligations. His wife also works, making a modest income that pays for family luxuries, like annual vacations, date nights, and the kids' summer activities. Bill makes enough to pay for the family's daily living expenses.

Bill always feels on edge and needs to cry. However, the past words of his Father echo in his mind, "Focus on solving the problem and don't cry about it! Be strong, someday you'll have a family that relies on you!" Bill also feels a need to connect more with his wife. They have a loving marriage, but he consistently feels quietly alone. Bill is unaware of this feeling, though it haunts him. The unconscious loneliness and "on edge" feelings guide his thoughts and actions. But to him, the problem is "not having enough time" and "no one will help me!" He quietly feels resentment because the family spends money on luxuries, and he is always worried about not having enough money or time for those luxuries.

Bill works throughout the day and night, often sacrificing his sleep. His marriage is eroding out from underneath him and his wife, though he is unaware of the erosion and his wife's worries about their relationship. She tries talking with him, and he responds, "Well, maybe if I could get a little help!" And, "It's just me! No one is helping me!" Bill focuses on work to alleviate his immense pressure and stress.

Our autonomic nervous system constantly scans for safety or danger and shifts up and down the Polyvagal ladder. As it shifts into and through the various Polyvagal states, the body will have an impulse that comes along with the state. In safety, the impulse is to connect with the self, others, and the environment; in sympathetic, to run or fight; in shutdown, to collapse with immobility.

There are impulses when climbing down the ladder and when climbing up the ladder. So, when attempting to self-regulate out of stuck trauma, the body will have an impulse based on what state it's in, followed by more impulses based on the state it's entering. Your body must climb the Polyvagal ladder sequentially: shutdown to fight, flight, and safety. This self-regulatory sequential shifting requires you to notice, feel, and then act on the impulse of each state.

Ladder climbing can be an intimidating and unnerving experience. You may not be familiar with the states and their experiences, and you may not consciously be aware of when your body is ready for the next step. Plus, your vagal brake may not be strong enough to tolerate the new experiences from each shift.

Each state has unique impulses. If those impulses are not allowed and used, they linger in the system. You likely remain stuck if you don't mindfully notice, feel, and act on your stuck state impulses.
Look back at Bill's short vignette. Do you notice any self-regulation impulses he ignores?

Bill feels two clear self-regulation impulses: crying and connecting with his wife. Crying is his body's attempt to release years and years of emotions: rejected, alone, on edge, and more. Connecting with his wife would help him receive co-regulation and anchor into safety. Both of these strategies would help him self-regulate, but he does not act on them and is likely not aware of them.

Bill also had the impulse to connect with his Father as a child. Young Bill wanted to play and bond with his dad, though these impulses to connect were repeatedly rebuffed. Young Bill's safety state and vagal brake could have been stronger, leading to healthier attachment and improved emotional regulation throughout life. Bill chronically lived in defense due to the severed connection and the tense nature of home.

When in any Polyvagal state, it's essential to feel its experience: yes, that includes the defensive states, even though it's difficult. When you do, the defensive state impulses emerge. If you act on the state's autonomic impulse, the autonomic nervous system can continue climbing the Polyvagal ladder.

The stuck state presents as a variety of persistent emotions: sorrow, despair, panic, rage, anger, anxiety, and more. These are all perfectly natural reactions to being stuck in a defensive state. Feeling these emotions can be challenging at first. Eventually, you will build the capacity to feel and welcome them while grounded in your safety state. But as of now, you're probably avoiding those emotions.

We typically avoid these difficult emotions through some sort of action: a behavioral adaptation. It's something we do to avoid feeling the discomfort of being in a defensive state or of shifting up the Polyvagal ladder. Even though we want to climb the ladder, doing so is vulnerable and leaves us feeling exposed. Feelings and memories will cause a neuroception of danger and return us down the ladder. Being able to tolerate the experience of these states and ladder climbing is essential to getting unstuck. To tolerate and welcome the experiences, we must stay firmly anchored in our ventral vagal safety state.

But instead of feeling into the defensive energy, one engages in some sort of behavior. Substance use is an obvious one. It relieves the pain and/or may give a pseudo ladder climb. Cutting and other forms of self-harm may relieve shutdown and trigger sympathetic activation but can also act as a distraction or a numbing agent to already-triggered freeze or sympathetic. These and other behavioral adaptations don't solve the problem, but they provide temporary relief. Other examples of behavioral adaptations are:

blocks.h3: Does Bill have a behavioral adaptation?

blocks.p: Look back at Bill's short vignette. Do you notice any behavioral adaptations?

Bill has one clear behavioral adaptation, just like his Father: overworking. He intensely focuses his defensive activation on work, even though he probably doesn't need to. His overworking is not a functional behavior; it's a means to divert his stuck defensive state away from experiencing it directly.

Cognitive adaptations are top-down skills to cope with the pains of a stuck defensive state. It's the same as a behavioral adaptation, but rather than body-based, it's brain-based. Cognitive adaptations reduce defensive dysregulation. Dr. Porges does not specifically differentiate cognitive or behavioral adaptations, so this is my own insertion into the theory I have not seen elsewhere.

Cognitive adaptations combine a couple of things: cognitive stories and cognitive skills. The cognitive story is the narrative that follows the Polyvagal state ("I'm unlovable," "It's my fault"). The cognitive skill flavors the story. These are some examples of cognitive skills:

Cognitive skills don't follow the Polyvagal state in the same way that cognitive stories do. The Polyvagal state uses cognitive skills, but the skills change based on the state's influence. For example, let's look at the cognitive skill of minimization: reducing the intensity or importance of something.

ul: Minimizing through shutdown: "It's not a big deal. It doesn't really matter anyway. Nothing will change."
Minimizing through fight: "It's not a big deal; get over it already! Why do you have to make it such a big thing?!"
Minimizing through flight: "It's not a big deal. I'll do better next time, I promise! It's okay; it's okay. Please don't be mad."
Minimizing through safety: "It's really not a big deal. Anyone could have discovered time travel, but thank you. I'm glad I got to do my part."

blocks.p: Each of these involves minimizing, but they sound a lot different. The person's state flavors the skill's use. However, the skill is still accessible in any state. So, cognitive skills help cope with or manage defensive states, especially when combined with a story. For example, when the skill of minimization combines with a story, it sounds like this: "It's not a big deal. I'll never succeed, so it's not worth trying. I always fail and always will."

Combining a cognitive skill and a cognitive story creates a cognitive adaptation. Like behavioral adaptations, cognitive adaptations don't help the individual self-regulate. If anything, they perpetuate the stuck defensive state. The behavior of substance use provides temporary relief. The cognition of "It doesn't matter anyway" does the same. Both result in the individual avoiding their inner experience.

Cognitive adaptations come before, during, or after behavioral ones. The cognitions can lead to a behavior, and the behavior can lead to cognitions. Or they can co-occur, both stemming from a dysregulated state. Regardless of which leads to the next, cognitions and behaviors continually reinforce each other and the defensive state. Drinking to excess reinforces negative self-concept, which reinforces the drinking, and so on. The state doesn't change, providing the dysregulated foundation for the perpetual reinforcement of behavior and cognition.

blocks.h3: Does Bill have a cognitive adaptation?

blocks.p: Look back at Bill's short vignette. Do you notice any cognitive adaptations?
Let's break them down in terms of skills and stories.
"Well, maybe if I could get a little help!" and "It's just me! No one is helping me!"

ul: Story = no one is there for him; he needs help

blocks.p: "Focus on solving the problem and don't cry about it! Be strong, someday you'll have a family that relies on you!"

ul: Story = the family will fail without self-sacrifice; crying is weakness

blocks.p: Humans isolate and keep secrets; animals don't. After we endure something horrific, we often just keep it to ourselves. This can be due to numerous things; here's a non-exhaustive list:

ul: fear of rejection by individual or group
fear of losing access to something

blocks.p: And so we keep it inside. We don't share what happened, even with people who could help. With my client populations over the years, the traumatic things they have been through have left them with a handful, if not all, of the above factors all at once. They feel shame or embarrassment at what they have gone through and don't want to re-experience the event by talking about it. If they speak up, their families might reject them, or the offending person might retaliate against them in some way.

Isolation is something that we do to ourselves by withholding truthful danger from others and getting help. Isolation is also a tool of the perpetrator. Imposing physical or emotional isolation through threats, intimidation, or psychological manipulation ensures that they will not be discovered and can continue with what they are doing. This is in no way a blaming of the victim here. This is not a judgment of what is good or bad or what they should or should not do. It's simply what happens far too often and something that reinforces a traumatic state.

We isolate and keep secrets by not speaking up about what we have been through, but we also isolate emotionally. We keep the events to ourselves, but we also keep the feelings to ourselves. We use behavioral and cognitive adaptations to suppress our emotions. These serve to keep the emotional pain at bay but end up making things worse in the long run. These emotions don't just disappear. They seem to not only stay but get worse. They fester and compound over time.

When I explain this concept to my clients, they know all too well how accurate it is. They nod in agreement because they feel it inside of them. Despite their best efforts to avoid the emotional pain, it just gets worse. It's not just the emotion. The emotion is tied to a Polyvagal state, one that is stuck. And if the stuck state is not dealt with, the emotions don't change.

Instead of isolating ourselves and our feelings, we need to actually connect with others. Eventually. It is not easy at first. But this is what needs to happen. We are social animals. We need each other. We need the co-regulation that safe others offer. This helps us to not only feel emotional relief but to begin to climb out of our stuck state.

The gazelle that survives an attack from a lion does not isolate itself. It returns to its herd and accepts their co-regulation. I know it's not that simple for us humans, and I make no attempts to minimize that. The other gazelles aren't going to blame them for the attack. The other gazelles aren't going to judge them. That's part of the problem for us humans: not only do we keep ourselves stuck in trauma on an individual level, but also on the familial and larger social level.

blocks.h3: Does Bill isolate and keep secrets?

blocks.p: Look back at Bill's short vignette. Do you notice any ways Bill isolates or keeps secrets?

Bill keeps his emotions and his needs to himself. He doesn't talk to his wife about how he feels. He doesn't seek out support from a friend or a professional. He doesn't even acknowledge that he is struggling emotionally. Instead, he uses his behavioral and cognitive adaptations. He literally isolates himself, focusing on work and separating from his wife and children, even late into the night.

Look, I think human beings are overall pretty amazing. But we also tend to make life more difficult for each other. And we do so on small scales, like between two people, larger scales, like familial, and even larger, like social. Not only do we directly traumatize each other (i.e., abuse and assault), but we also directly and indirectly ensure that we keep each other in a traumatized state, like through victim-blaming and marginalizing entire groups of people.

The interpersonal and the social affect you and have a big hand in sculpting who you are. This hugely depends on the context you are born into and the systems you are a part of. If you are a woman that is born in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, your experience will probably be a lot different than a woman born in the United States. And even then, a woman born into a fundamentalist religious family will probably have a different experience than one born into a socially progressive family in a coastal city like San Francisco. (Although the belief systems of both of these familial structures will be passed on, even forcefully. Both of these structures will have a concept of a woman's role and how they fit into the family and society at large.)

The beliefs passed or forced onto you will directly affect your self-regulating capacity. The individual that is taught to "suck it up" or "be strong," will probably have less likelihood of feeling their state nonjudgmentally or with curiosity. My Hispanic clients over the years, in particular, report this, though the "be strong" mentality is pretty widespread across gender and culture. (It's also just wrong. Anyone can "be strong" by avoiding their pain. In my opinion, it takes real strength to deal with your pain through acknowledgment and eventually feeling it.)

The individual who is taught to be a certain way or else it'll betray their identity will have less likelihood of following their biological impulses toward things that bring them safety and happiness. The little girl who is taught not to be a "tomboy" isn't going to follow their impulses to run and use their healthy aggression. The boy who embraces a stereotypically feminine aspect of himself, like nurturance or decoration, might be shamed away from liking "girl stuff."

All of these imposed beliefs serve as an obstacle to someone who is attempting to find out who they are and what they are pulled toward. These pulls are potential safety anchors, which are likely to help them feel in their bodies, feel their feelings, access safety, and build connections. The imposed beliefs serve to reinforce some bulls**t expectations of the person imposing the beliefs. It says more about the imposer than the one imposed upon.

The person imposing is dealing with their own stuck state as well. Rather, not dealing with it. We could argue that focusing on controlling the outside world (i.e., the person they don't approve of) is their own cognitive and behavioral adaptation. Instead of dealing with their own stuck state, they focus on controlling others. That way, they don't have to feel their own pain. They externalize it at the expense of someone else. They create and reinforce stuck states in others to gain relief from their own. This doesn't work, of course. They don't receive any healing or ladder climbing.

This creates an imposition on others through force and coercion. The force could be through outright threats and physical aggression. This force could also be through shame, humiliation, embarrassment, and other emotionally aggressive tactics. Force could be through social ostracization as well. The person imposing beliefs might reject "the other" or enlist a system to aid the rejection, like the larger family or relative system.

More people are involved to further complicate this dynamic between imposer and imposed. Third-party individuals go along with or directly support the person imposing. This adds to the imposer's feelings of superiority and righteousness, further emboldening them. The third-party people otherwise might not have a strong opinion on the matter: at least not enough to act on and impose their own beliefs. But they are swayed by the imposer's power and charisma.

The point is that our beliefs may be the cognitive imposition of another, even our most personal and cherished ones. And these beliefs can stifle our potential to climb our ladder and anchor in safety.

blocks.h3: Does Bill repeat imposed belief systems?

blocks.p: Look back at Bill's short vignette. Do you notice any ways Bill repeats imposed belief systems?

Of course, he does. He repeats the imposed beliefs of his own Father: don't cry because it makes him weak, his family's well-being is entirely up to him, sacrifice himself to no end. And Bill surely has imposed beliefs from his political, religious, cultural, and other social-level organizations.

Polyvagal state shifts have no inherent value. They're simply the bodily organism's way of increasing the chances of survival, and thus increasing the chances of reproducing that strand of genetic material for another generation. There is no judgment or value assigned to this. It's simply the mechanics of evolution.

Despite this simple and natural truth, humans seem to have lost the capacity to be with their bodily sensations. We need to learn and practice this. Animals don't need to. They're at one with their bodies.

Humans do all the things that I've listed above and a lot more. We've created lives where we strive to rid ourselves of self-regulation. We don't want to feel our states. Instead, we focus on what we do or do not have. We focus on what others are or are not doing. We focus on what we think needs to change in society and then evangelize in our social media comment sections. We seek incessant entertainment or distraction from what is happening within. We've become fixated on the external and complete strangers to the internal. And I believe we are more "connected" with our digital personas than ourselves; to our projected anonymous identities and not our actual bodies.

Don't think you're a stranger to yourself? Okay. When is the last time you checked comments on your social media? When is the last time you mindlessly watched something? Got it? Okay, now ask yourself when is the last time you noticed your breath?

I regularly ask my clients, "How's your breathing?" And they regularly tell me, "I never noticed it until you asked!" We don't check in with ourselves. We don't notice our breath, our emotions, our feelings of safety, and on and on.

We're strangers to ourselves. So when autonomic shifts occur, we have no idea what is happening. We don't know how to notice it, how to feel it, or how to tolerate it. Our vagal brakes are not developed enough to handle them and allow natural autonomic self-regulation to occur.

blocks.why: When is the last time you noticed your breath? This practice is a few minutes of noticing, without changing anything.

blocks.p: Our safety pathways are underused. Instead, the defensive pathways are probably overused. Overused from numerous different sources:

ul: outright traumatic events in our lives
outright oppression from one group to another
advertising that stokes our fears to compel a specific behavior

blocks.p: We live in states of defense. We scrutinize ourselves and each other. We judge, label, otherize, and manipulate... all to fulfill some sort of desire to feel dominant, satiated, protected, or like we belong.

We're strangers to ourselves: on a personal level and on an interpersonal level. We can't handle the personal st inside, and then we definitely can't handle the interpersonal st outside. It all becomes alien to us.

But really, it's just biology. It's just our internal stuff trying its damndest to self-regulate and optimize bodily resources. It's the cues of safety or danger that we give to and receive from each other. It's not that complex to understand. Luckily, we can learn what's happening and what to do about it. But we have a very, very hard time executing all of it.

blocks.h3: Does Bill seem like a stranger to himself?

blocks.p: Look back at Bill's short vignette. Do you notice any ways Bill is a stranger to himself?

Heck, yes, he is. Bill has almost no idea what's happening within him. He is unaware of his lingering loneliness and his need to connect. He's stuck in behavioral and cognitive adaptations day after day.

blocks.h: How do you keep yourself stuck?

blocks.p: Bill's gotten enough attention. Now it's your turn. It's difficult to turn your attention to yourself. Well, sort of... I have no doubt you can nitpick every last minutia of what is wrong with yourself when you're in a defensive state. But can you self-reflect with honest self-compassion from your safety state? If not, this next section and journal opportunity might be too much. But it's also an important piece of crafting a new self-narrative.

I don't expect you to notice all of the ways you keep yourself stuck. Some, if not most, are unconscious. They're out of your awareness for the time being. But some might be easily recognizable. In fact, they are probably what brought you here. There's something that you want to change, like a behavior or a thought.
You don't need to reflect on the why of keeping yourself stuck. And you don't need to reflect on the history of it either. Instead, focus on the facts. Here are some examples:

ul: "Yelling at my children contributes to my stuckness."

blocks.p: If it's easier, let's break this up into a few questions:

ol: Is there a behavior you want to change? (yes or no)
Does this behavior help keep you stuck? (yes or no)

blocks.p: Now, put these together:
And that's it. Nothing more. Nothing less. It's just a factual statement. Do the best you can not to evaluate or judge the behavior. Judgment and evaluation can sound like this:

ul: "[Behavior] contributes to my stuckness and it'll never change."
"[Behavior] contributes to my stuckness and I'm so worthless."

blocks.p: If you notice evaluations or judgments, write them down in your journal. Then, cross off the evaluation or judgment. Like this:

ul: "[Behavior] contributes to my stuckness<s> and it'll never change</s>."
"[Behavior] contributes to my stuckness <s>and I'm so worthless.</s>"

blocks.p: If you like, add a message of hope to the end. Like this:

ul: "[Behavior] contributes to my stuckness and now I have new knowledge to work with to change it."
"[Behavior] contributes to my stuckness and I believe in myself."
"[Behavior] contributes to my stuckness and there's something I can do about it."

blocks.h: This has nothing to do with blame

blocks.p: Many things contribute to your stuckness, just like they did with Bill's. However, not all of them are within your control or capacity to directly influence. You can't make your spouse a better co-regulator, undo the past, or make your parents understand you.

Identifying a behavior contributing to your stuckness doesn't mean your stuckness is your fault. Or that if you simply stopped the behavior, your stuckness would resolve. It's simply a factual statement acknowledging something you're doing that reinforces the stuckness. Yes, your stuckness probably involves other people, your environment(s), and many social factors. However, making a change in your own life is up to you.

So, I'm not blaming you for your stuckness. And I don't want you to blame yourself for your stuckness either. But I do want you to acknowledge what you're doing that contributes to your stuckness. You can also acknowledge how others contribute, too. But the focus needs to be on yourself. You don't control anyone else. And the most positive change comes when you own as much of your journey as possible.

You have both behavioral and cognitive adaptations. If you want to focus on a cognitive adaptation, go ahead. But I find those are more difficult to notice without judgment and change. I encourage you to focus on a specific behavior. You can use this behavior as a measuring stick for your progress.

blocks.prompt: Are you able to reflect on your behavioral adaptations without blame and judgment?

blocks.h: Emotions leading to behavior and cognitive adaptations

blocks.p: Your behavioral and cognitive adaptations didn't appear out of nowhere. They aren't random, and you didn't plan them out. They stem from a defensive Polyvagal state: flight/fight, shutdown, freeze, appease, or fawn. For now, don't worry too much about the underlying Polyvagal state. You may not be able to feel it directly. Instead, let's focus on the emotions.

Your Polyvagal state leads to sensations, impulses, emotions, cognitions, and behaviors. The state, impulses, and sensations are typically unconscious and difficult to notice. Cognitions and emotions are more accessible to notice and reflect on. In the moment, not so much. But afterward, with self-compassion, yes.

When you engage in a behavioral adaptation, there is probably an emotion within you directly before (and during) the adaptation. Jackie feels sad and alone before isolating herself in her room and binge-watching TikTok. Roark feels overwhelmed when he comes home from work and then drinks beer in his chair all night. Mitchell feels stupid before he creates a distraction in class.
Let's identify your emotion(s) before you engage in your behavioral adaptation. If this is too much for you, come back another time when you are ready. Or, just move on.

blocks.prompt: Do you have a behavioral adaptation you engage in when you're dysregulated?
What emotion is driving the adaptation?
Fill in the brackets: "When I feel [emotion], I tend to [behavior] which contributes to my stuckness."
